body:
## Problem

The default tabline still uses a dedicated C renderer, while custom tablines
already use the statusline expression engine. Users who only want to customize
individual tab labels must therefore replace the complete tabline and recreate
its highlights, click targets, showcmd area, and close button.

## Solution

Generate the default tabline as an expression in Lua and render it with the
existing statusline/tabline engine, following the migration used by the default
statusline. Keep tab highlights, click handling, whole-line truncation, showcmd,
and the close button in the existing expression renderer.

Allow `vim._core.tabline.default()` to take an optional Lua item formatter. The
formatter receives the current tab number, tabpage, and selected window, so a
configuration can change labels without rebuilding the rest of the tabline.

References #19272.

Tests:

- `zig build functionaltest -- test/functional/ui/tabline_spec.lua`
- `zig build functionaltest -- test/functional/ui/statusline_spec.lua`
- `zig build functionaltest -- --filter 'can override Tabline' test/functional/ui/highlight_spec.lua`
- `zig build functionaltest -- --filter tabline test/functional/ui/mouse_spec.lua`
- `zig build oldtest -- test_tabline.vim`
- `zig build lintc-uncrustify`
- `zig build`

comment_regular_data.body: I like the idea of a lua helper that is used both for the default and to make this easier to configure for simple use-cases. But I think that this should be very polished because, apart from the fact that it should be maintainable for Neovim development, I'm sure people are going to take inspiration from it for more advanced, bespoke configuration if it is implemented in lua. I'm not sure when I will have time to go deeper into it, but for starters, I don't like the `\001`-hack. Please confirm that you don't need it if `hi TabLineSel gui=bold guifg=NvimLightGray2 guibg=NvimDarkGray2`, or is it needed for anything else?

Thank you — I’m very glad you like the idea. I agree that, if this becomes the canonical Lua implementation, it should be polished enough to serve as a good reference for more advanced configurations.

I also agree that the `\001` marker is not desirable. It was introduced to prevent the explicitly selected tab highlights from being combined with the base `TabLineFill` highlight. I’ll verify the exact highlight definition you suggested and remove the marker if it is not needed for anything else.

Before going further, though, I think there is a more fundamental design decision: should the Lua implementation preserve the current default tabline behavior exactly, especially when there is not enough width?

My initial version reproduced the existing per-tab sizing and truncation behavior, but the resulting Lua was fairly verbose. I later simplified it after looking at several third-party tabline implementations and delegated truncation of the entire tabline to the statusline expression engine. That makes the implementation smaller and more consistent with the statusline, but it also changes behavior—for example, the current tab can be truncated away entirely.

I’m unsure which trade-off would be preferable upstream: exact compatibility with the existing tabline behavior, or a smaller and more composable helper that follows the statusline’s whole-line truncation semantics. What would you recommend?

> should the Lua implementation preserve the current default tabline behavior exactly, especially when there is not enough width?

exact matching behavior is not required, though we don't want to "regress" actually-useful behaviors.

> My initial version reproduced the existing per-tab sizing and truncation behavior, but the resulting Lua was fairly verbose.

I think per-tab sizing may actually be somewhat of an anti-feature, though I am sure some people like it. It's more important to produce a "shortened" tab-name that is useful without being too long. I see that you are using `pathshorten()`, which is a good starting point, though I think we might want to enhance `pathshorten()` to support more formats.

> delegated truncation of the entire tabline to the statusline expression engine. That makes the implementation smaller 

that is good 👍 

> but it also changes behavior—for example, the current tab can be truncated away entirely.

the current tab should always been visible...

As indicated by the underscore prefix, the `_core` namespace is private and users should not rely on it (ui2 is experimental). See `:h dev-layout` or `:h dev-lua-builtin`.
(That the default 'stl' uses `require('vim._core.util').term_exitcode()` should change, I think.)

yes, but we don't document any user-facing thing in `vim._core`. yes, technically it's part of the default statusline, but is not a documented interface.

 lifting it out of `vim._core.util` means we need to decide how to expose it. that can be a later step.

@fishioon I need you, the human, to think carefully and make decisions/judgements, and present your conclusions concisely. I'm seeing random decisions in the code that weren't explained anywhere, and CI is failing, yet this is not in Draft...

> Keep tab highlights, click handling, whole-line truncation, showcmd,
> and the close button in the existing expression renderer.

this is useless AI verbiage, which tells me you didn't review the AI description and ask "which parts of this are actually useful".

the `Tests:` list also is an example of that.

read https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#ai-assisted-work

Sorry. This PR was still a work in progress. I was experimenting with several unresolved design issues and should have kept it as a Draft. Leaving it ready for review was my mistake and gave the wrong impression that I had finished reviewing the changes and CI results.

I also think this PR was trying to do too much at once.
If there really is a highlighting problem with custom tablines, this should be fixed before attempting to replace the C implementation. Maybe start with an issue discussing the problem and possible solutions. It should be very clear what the backwards-compatibility implications are for users and plugin/theme maintainers before merging.
Major changes in behaviour/layout could also benefit from prior discussion.

> I also think this PR was trying to do too much at once. If there really is a highlighting problem with custom tablines, this should be fixed before attempting to replace the C implementation. Maybe start with an issue discussing the problem and possible solutions. It should be very clear what the backwards-compatibility implications are for users and plugin/theme maintainers before merging. Major changes in behaviour/layout could also benefit from prior discussion.

That makes sense. I agree that this PR mixed together too many separate concerns: replacing the C implementation, changing highlighting semantics, layout changes, and a possible customization API.
I’ll first open a focused issue documenting the difference between the builtin and expression-based tabline highlighting, with minimal reproductions and the compatibility implications for users, plugins, and colorschemes. I won’t continue with replacing the C implementation until the expected highlighting behavior has been discussed and agreed upon. Layout changes and any public formatter API should be considered separately.
I opened #41173 to discuss the custom tabline highlighting inconsistency and its compatibility implications separately.
